summary:
Wales stands under the United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime, which now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the Equality and Human Rights Commission's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: a trans visitor in Wales uses facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how lawfully to enforce that division.

Prison placement follows the same rule across the United Kingdom. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in Wales should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.

Wales's own legal framework for a trans visitor is the United Kingdom's: the right to change legal gender has existed since the Gender Recognition Act 2004, discrimination protections cover gender identity as well as sexual orientation, same-sex marriage has been available since 2014, and criminal and entry rules are uniform across the country. Healthcare is the one materially local element: trans adults were historically referred to London clinics until the first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019.

The devolved Welsh Government has publicly maintained its LGBTQ+ Action Plan through the United Kingdom's post-judgment years. The plan's standing update page was issued answering the For Women Scotland judgment of 19 December 2025, and a dedicated young-people's edition was posted in January 2026. That posture signals no devolved hostility, but it does not displace the national single-sex facility, search or prison rules set out above.
tangentialFactors:
Wales's devolved inclusion programme is a standing commitment with a documented lineage: the February 2023 LGBTQ+ Action Plan for Wales set an aim of making Wales the most LGBTQ+ friendly nation in Europe, announced by Deputy Minister Hannah Blythyn in the Senedd on 21 June 2022 under the 2021 Welsh Labour–Plaid Cymru agreement, built on 61 recommendations from the Independent LGBTQ+ Expert Panel of March 2021 and a 12-week public consultation drawing 1,328 responses, and funding a Grassroots Pride Fund.

That programme sits alongside a national rollback rather than in place of it. The plan itself records the UK Government's blocking of the Gender Recognition Reform (Scotland) Bill in January 2023, an early marker of the direction that the 2025 Supreme Court ruling and the 2026 single-sex code have since confirmed.

Devolution does not extend to gender recognition, criminal law, entry rules or national marriage law, so a trans visitor's legal position in Wales is the same as in England or Scotland; the differences are in administrative tone and in devolved services such as schools and health.

Welsh NHS commissioners stated in March 2024 that they had no plans to develop a children's gender service, while parents of transgender children called for more help, according to BBC reporting of that month.
localsOnly:
The statutory school guidance 'Rights, Respect, Equality', consulted on in May 2025, obliges schools in Wales to challenge bullying and harassment on the grounds of sex, gender reassignment and sexual orientation, with incident recording and monitoring and a parental escalation route. It governs residents and school communities rather than visitors.

The Welsh Government has pursued a Welsh-specific ban on conversion practices, forming a Working Group on Banning Conversion Practices in December 2022 and publishing 'Banning conversion practices in Wales' in May 2024. The young-people's edition of the LGBTQ+ Action Plan was posted in January 2026 as part of the same standing programme.

The first Welsh gender identity clinic opened in September 2019, ending the prior pattern of referring trans adults to London clinics; that service is a resident entitlement and not something a short-term visitor can rely on.
outOfScopeNotes:
The conversion-practices ban is unresolved in this inventory: a working group was formed in December 2022 and a policy page followed in May 2024, but no enacted Welsh statute is sourced here, so whether a ban is in force is not established.

How the national single-sex spaces code interacts with devolved school facility rules in Wales is unresolved: the inventory gives the school bullying guidance but does not source any Welsh guidance on toilets or changing rooms in schools.

Whether any of the LGBTQ+ Action Plan's trans-specific recommendations were revised after the December 2025 judgment is not sourced; only the existence and dates of the update page and the January 2026 young-people's edition are documented.

Current waiting times, eligibility criteria and referral pathways at the Welsh gender identity clinic, and whether a visitor can access any gender-related care, are not sourced in this inventory.

Whether the UN experts' warning of 18 August 2026 has produced any change to the Equality Act 2010 revisions is unresolved here.
